common_name: Ivory Silk Japanese Tree Lilac (Compact Heavy-Blooming Tree Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in full sun in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Ivory Silk is a grafted selection valued for a denser, more compact, more uniformly rounded-pyramidal habit and heavier, more reliable bloom than seed-grown Japanese tree lilac, and it tolerates urban conditions including compacted soil, heat, and pollution once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Ivory Silk is the most widely planted selection of Japanese tree lilac, prized for a denser, more compact, and more symmetrically rounded-pyramidal crown than seed-grown trees, along with heavier and more consistent flowering at a younger age. In June, two to three weeks after common lilacs finish, it produces massive creamy-white flower panicles up to 12 inches long in great abundance, creating a cloud-like display when the familiar spring shrub lilacs have long since faded. The fragrance is heavier and more privet-like than the sweet scent of common lilac, which some find less appealing but which does not diminish the tree's landscape value. Reddish-brown, lightly exfoliating, cherry-like bark provides attractive winter interest on mature specimens. Exceptionally cold-hardy (to zone 3) and highly resistant to the powdery mildew that plagues common lilac, Ivory Silk is largely trouble-free and widely used as a street tree, specimen lawn tree, and small shade tree in northern climates.

common_name: Happy Wanderer Hardenbergia (Vigorous Deep-Purple Coral Pea Vine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade against a fence, trellis, or arbor; Happy Wanderer is the most widely available and most vigorous false sarsaparilla selection, climbing readily by twining stems.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade with a fence, trellis, or arbor for support; Happy Wanderer is the best-known and most widely sold selection of false sarsaparilla, a vigorous, fast-growing, twining vine that can climb 10 to 16 feet given support. In late winter and early spring it produces a spectacular, dense flush of small, sweet-pea-shaped flowers in rich, deep violet-purple with a small contrasting white-and-yellow mark at the center of each standard petal, borne in long, cascading racemes of 20 or more blooms against dark, leathery, evergreen trifoliate leaves. The bloom timing provides vivid color during the coldest, dullest part of the garden year in mild climates and attracts bees and honeyeating birds. Tolerant of considerable neglect and moderate drought once established, it thrives with minimal care on fences, pergolas, and banks in zones 8-11, but is frost-tender and should be given wind and cold protection at the northern edge of its range.

common_name: Aztec Pearl Mexican Orange Blossom (Narrow-Leaved Pink-Budded Choisya Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; Aztec Pearl, a hybrid of Choisya ternata and C. arizonica, is somewhat more compact and slightly more cold-tolerant than the straight species, though it still benefits from a sheltered, south- or west-facing site at the northern edge of its range.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; Aztec Pearl is a hybrid of Mexican orange blossom (Choisya ternata) and the narrower-leaved Choisya arizonica, bred by Hilliers Nurseries and awarded the RHS Award of Garden Merit. It is distinguished from the species by narrow, finely divided, almost willowy trifoliate leaflets that give the whole shrub a lighter, more feathery texture, and by clusters of star-shaped white flowers that open from pink-tinged buds in spring, with a strong, sweet fragrance carrying notes of orange blossom, and frequently reblooming again in late summer or fall. The aromatic foliage releases a sharp citrus scent when crushed. Slightly more compact and, by most accounts, a touch more cold-hardy than the species, it still benefits from winter protection at the cold edge of its range. An excellent choice for mixed borders, foundation plantings, and containers where its fine texture and fragrance can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Grace Ward Lithodora (Large-Flowered Deep Blue Lithodora)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky, acidic soil in full sun; Grace Ward is propagated by cuttings and is intolerant of alkaline soils and poorly drained conditions, exactly as the species is.

directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Grace Ward is widely regarded as the finest-flowered lithodora selection, bearing unusually large, saturated, gentian-blue trumpet flowers held just above a low, spreading, woody-based mat of small, dark green, evergreen leaves. It holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit and flowers heavily in spring and early summer, with sporadic rebloom later in the season. As with the species, it strictly requires acidic, sharply drained soil and collapses quickly in alkaline or heavy, wet ground, and it performs best where summers are cool and humid, such as the Pacific Northwest or coastal climates, struggling in hot, humid inland regions. An outstanding choice for rock gardens, dry walls, and raised bed edges where its intense blue color can spill over stone.

common_name: Brazen Hussy Lesser Celandine (Bronze-Leaved Yellow-Flowered Celandine)

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers or divisions in fall, 1-2 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade under deciduous trees; unlike the wild species, Brazen Hussy sets little or no viable seed and spreads much more slowly, but it should still be planted in a contained bed away from streams, floodplains, and natural areas as a precaution.

directions: Plant tubers or divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled sun beneath deciduous trees; Brazen Hussy is a celebrated named selection of lesser celandine, discovered and introduced by the plantsman Christopher Lloyd at Great Dixter, distinguished by glossy, near-black, bronze-purple foliage that forms a striking low carpet in earliest spring, sharply contrasting with the bright, glistening, buttercup-yellow flowers held just above it. Like the species it is a fleeting spring ephemeral, emerging and flowering before deciduous tree canopies leaf out and then dying back completely underground by early summer, at which point its location should be marked. Crucially, Brazen Hussy sets little or no viable seed and increases far more slowly by tuber than the wild type, making it a well-behaved choice for woodland gardens and shaded borders where the species itself would be an aggressive, invasive spreader. Even so, it should be kept in contained beds well away from streams and wild areas.

common_name: James Roof Silk Tassel Bush (Extra-Long-Catkin Male Silk Tassel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; James Roof is a male-only clone selected for exceptionally long catkins and performs best in cool, moist coastal climates with dry summers, establishing poorly from transplants in summer heat and drought.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; James Roof is the most widely grown selection of silk tassel bush, a male clone named for the East Bay Regional Parks botanist who selected it, prized for producing the longest and most abundant catkins of any silk tassel bush cultivar — long, silky, silvery pale gray-green catkins reaching up to 14 inches that drape from the branch tips from December into February, when the entire shrub appears wrapped in cascading silver-gray fringe. Because it is a male selection it produces no berries, but the catkin display alone makes it the standard bearer of the species in cultivation. The leathery, wavy-margined, glossy deep green leaves with woolly gray undersides give the plant good year-round texture. Native to coastal California chaparral, it is drought-tolerant once established and resents excessive summer irrigation, performing best in mild, coastal-influenced climates. An outstanding specimen for dry gardens, woodland edges, and shrub borders that need winter interest.

common_name: Cousin Itt River Wattle (Ultra-Compact Ground-Hugging Weeping Acacia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Cousin Itt is an extremely compact, ground-hugging selection of river wattle that keeps its low mounding form without pruning, unlike the tree-form species.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Cousin Itt is an extremely popular dwarf selection of river wattle, forming a dense, low, completely ground-hugging mound only 12 to 18 inches tall but spreading 3 to 5 feet, made up of the same fine-textured, cascading, bright-green, needle-like phyllodes as the species arranged in a rounded, shaggy dome that is widely compared to the cartoon character it is named for. It is grown almost entirely for its distinctive textural form rather than its small, pompom-like yellow spring flowers, and it works well as a dramatic textural groundcover, a cascading accent spilling over a wall or large container, or a low border specimen. More moisture-tolerant than most acacias but still requiring good drainage, it is native in habit to the stream banks of southeastern Australia and needs minimal maintenance once established.

common_name: Kohout's Ice Breaker Korean Fir (Ultra-Dwarf Silver-Backed Mounding Fir)

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Kohout's Ice Breaker is an extreme dwarf sport of 'Silberlocke' and, like its parent, does not tolerate hot, dry summers well and prefers cool, moist growing conditions.

directions: Kohout's Ice Breaker is an extreme dwarf sport of the popular Korean fir cultivar 'Silberlocke', sharing the same upturned needles that flash their bright silvery-white undersides, but carried on a dramatically more compact, slow-growing, irregularly mounding to semi-prostrate plant that gains only an inch or two of height per year. Over a decade or more it forms a dense, low, silver-flecked mound ideally suited to rock gardens, trough and container plantings, and dwarf conifer collections where a full-sized Korean fir would be far too large. Like the species and 'Silberlocke', it can begin producing upright, ornamental, purple-violet cones that fade through blue to brown even while still quite small. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it the cool, humid conditions it needs since it performs poorly in hot, dry summer climates. Extremely slow growth and long lifespan make it a prized specimen for gardeners with limited space.

common_name: Tamariscifolia Savin Juniper (Tam Juniper, Classic Low-Spreading Blue-Green Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; Tamariscifolia, commonly called tam juniper, is one of the most widely planted low-growing evergreen shrubs in North American commercial landscaping. WARNING: all parts are poisonous — do not plant where children may ingest the berries.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; tam juniper is one of the most widely planted low-growing evergreen shrubs in North American commercial and residential landscaping, forming a dense, irregular, layered mound of soft-textured, blue-green foliage that rises 18 to 30 inches tall while spreading 8 to 12 feet or more with age, considerably wider than it is tall. It tolerates heat, cold, drought, and poor rocky or sandy soils with ease, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings, parking lot islands, banks, and slopes, but it is prone to root and crown rot in wet, poorly drained sites and should never be overwatered. As with the species, the crushed foliage has a distinctly pungent, unpleasant odor rather than the pleasant cedar scent of most junipers, and all parts are poisonous if ingested.

common_name: Emerald Sea Shore Juniper (Bright Green Mounding Coastal Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in sandy, well-drained, even infertile soil in full sun; Emerald Sea is a bright green-needled shore juniper selection with a somewhat more mounding, less prostrate habit than 'Blue Pacific', and it tolerates salt spray and poor sandy soils equally well.

directions: Plant in dry, sandy, well-drained to poor soil in full sun; Emerald Sea is a bright green-needled selection of shore juniper, distinguished from the more common blue-green cultivars like 'Blue Pacific' by its cheerful, consistently bright green color and a slightly more mounding, less flat-to-the-ground habit, rising 12 to 18 inches tall as it spreads. Like the species, it is native in character to sandy coastal cliffs and beaches and is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, wind, drought, and nutrient-poor soils, making it an excellent choice for coastal gardens, seaside slopes, and hot, sandy bank stabilization. The needles are notably sharp and prickly, so it should be sited away from paths and walkways. Because it holds its bright green color through winter rather than taking on the purplish or bronze tones some junipers show, it is valued where a cheerful, consistent green groundcover is wanted year-round. Largely free of serious pests and diseases in the hot, dry conditions where many other groundcovers struggle.
